items.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production."


Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... 
[Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

items.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News, which is liveblogging all the videogame history happening after GTA 6's Thursday launch. 
Like how singer The Weeknd says he found his real-life mansion appearing in the game... How players found a glitch that apparently lets you override the game's third-person point of view to play in first-person. And apparently it's also possible to jack an old woman's mobility scooter. (Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...)

- The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog. Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski... Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard... 

 — GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games. Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores. Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week. The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. 
- Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads.
 



Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News. Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC. And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access." At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported. PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.]	 

Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game. 

But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed:

The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop." Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.

items.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet:
Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] 


Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. 
Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. 

But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle:

 Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" 
Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city."

Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety.
One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... 

The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles." 

Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.

items.title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palintir Employees in California
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian. 

The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."

 The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working... 

In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station.
 

The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV.

The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. 

After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit... 

If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.

items.title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The Prisoner is getting a remake, reports ScreenRant. "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..."

ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. 

You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." 

More details on the remake from ScreenRant:
 Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized... 

It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. 
Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.

items.title: Americans Enters Post-Penny World, Businesses Now Allowed to Round Cash Transactions to Nearest Nickel
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Friday U.S. President Trump "signed the Common Cents Act, which now lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law," reports CBS News:

It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents... Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. 
CBS includes this quote from an official NACS, an advocacy group for the convenience/fuel retailing industry. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended. 

 NBC News points out that the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector's versions of pennies in "limited quantities," reporting on what has and hasn't changed now:

The penny can still be used as legal tender "for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues," according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence "for as long as possible...." And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.

items.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." 

Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.)

Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." 


Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." 


The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. 

While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts." 

"I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."

items.title: Nvidia's Accounting Practices Now Being Investigated by America's SEC
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
We knew America's Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating Nvidia.
But Reuters reported Friday that what's being investigated is Nvidia's accounting practices, according to "two people briefed on the matter."


Prices of Nvidia shares extended losses and were down about 13% on Friday, according to LSEG data, after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe. They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report... The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month. 

Reuters says they "could not immediately determine" exactly what potential accounting issues America's SEC is examining." (And Reuters points out that "Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.") 

Their article adds some historical context — that U.S. authorities "have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week." And the Financial Times reported Tuesday that Nvidia removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown of revenue sources, Reuters points out, "even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue."

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers... Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks. On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

items.title: Earth has a New Moon
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN:

Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. 

The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. 


While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... 

The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

items.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
 
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED.
 
"We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

items.title: Scientists Discover New and Horrible Eagle-Based Way Our Ancestors Died
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot. 

Eagle-eyeing you…for dinner!

Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known. 

Birds of prey (raptors) have hunted primates for at least 20 million years, including early human relatives, known as hominins. For example, a hominin toddler known as the “Taung child” shows signs of being killed by a raptor roughly 2.5 million years ago. But scientists have assumed that hominins outgrew their status as bird bites since that time, and there are no reports of raptors preying on primates that weigh over 28 pounds on record—until now. 

In 2025, scientists discovered that Verreaux’s eagles—one of the largest eagle species in the world—at Ennedi Plateau in Chad are likely hunting adult olive baboons weighing up to 57 pounds. The team found baboon remains among the region’s sandstone cliffs that show signature marks of eagle predation, such as talon punctures on the skull and scrapes to the shoulder bones.

“We cannot definitively rule out scavenging activity, but the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” said researchers led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St. Andrews. The team also observed the baboons rapidly retreat when eagles approached, suggesting that they feared aerial attacks.

Some researchers have argued against the “raptor-mediated predation” of the Taung child on the grounds that the hominin would have been too heavy for a bird. The study’s authors get extra points for including a quote from the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail on this point: “It is a simple question of weight ratios. A five-ounce bird could not carry a 1-pound coconut.” IYKYK.

However, the laughs stop there, as the team refutes this idea by recounting the grisly “low flight with sustained grip attack” that eagles perform on ungulates, such as antelopes or cattle, which reveal that raptors can kill animals that are many times their own weight with the right approach. 

“Briefly, an eagle will land on the back or neck of a moderately large ungulate, gripping it firmly with its talons. If the prey withstands knocking to the ground, the eagle will ride it with wings outstretched and flapping to maintain balance until the quarry collapses, either from exhaustion, shock, or internal injury. A similar tactic is described in the of a Harpy eagle ( attacking a 52-kg adult woman.”

Wow, new fear unlocked! Imagine being an early hominin, minding your own business banging rocks together or something, when suddenly a giant bird of prey either pushes you off a cliff or rides you to death. For everyone preparing to eat a huge bird for Thanksgiving next week, be grateful that it’s no longer the other way around.

Speaking of unwieldy meals, scientists have captured an unprecedented glimpse of a star eating another star, thereby forming a new mega-star. 

Over the past few years, scientists noticed that something weird has been unfolding in a binary star system called AT 2025abao—nicknamed “Bao” (yum!)—in the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, which is about 2.5 million miles away from the Milky Way. One of the stars, “Big Bao,” was expanding into its dying red giant phase, which pulled its companion, “Little Bao,” into a deadly spiral. Last year, the system rapidly brightened, signaling that Big Bao had swallowed Little Bao.

“In October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption” and exhibited “a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K,” said researchers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University. The system “shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae,a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection…during the merger of a star with its companion.”

“This inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly,” the team noted. 

Congratulations to the newly-fed couple! Long may Bao shine.

Girl, put your records on / but don’t think you own that song

We’ve all had that feeling of hearing a familiar song and being transported to a specific time and place in our lives. But as it turns out, the recollections stirred by those cherished songs are probably not all that special, according to a new study that surveyed 233 undergraduate students about these so-called “music-evoked autobiographical memories.”

The students (aged 18-23) listened to clips of grouped into two categories: “new” songs released from 2014 to 2019, during their adolescence, and “old” songs released from 1985 to 1995, before they were born. When asked to reminisce about the songs, students with similar backgrounds were remarkably aligned in their answers.

“Memories evoked by country songs were more strongly associated with very recent time periods (college) and themes relating to family, driving, summertime, romantic partners, and listening to music (particularly music selected by someone else),” said researchers led by Cara Turnbull of Texas Tech University. 

“Alternatively, memories evoked by hip-hop songs were most often associated with friends, acquaintances (such as classmates, coworkers, and teammates), dancing, and being at school, while those evoked by pop songs were most associated with middle school, listening at home or by oneself, and singing along,” the team added. 

As an elder millennial, it was humbling to realize what counts as an “oldie” these days. I also felt my generation’s soundtrack was done dirty by offerings like “Achy Breaky Heart” by Billy Ray Cyrus or “Whoomp! There it is” by Tag Team. No Stevie Nicks? Madonna? Wu Tang? All I ask of future generations is that you do not judge us solely by the croonings of C+C Music Factory and Bryan Adams, I beg you. 

Join hands, dear friends, for we are about to run directly through majestic fountains of whale snot. Scientists who flew drones through whale “blow”—the mucus-filled vapor exhaled by whales through their blowholes—have successfully sequenced whole genomes from the snotty samples, representing “a major step towards non-invasive cetacean sampling,” according to a new study.

“Preserving biodiversity requires the genetic monitoring of wild populations, which is traditionally done through invasive sampling techniques for DNA collection,” said researchers led by Éadin O’Mahony of the University of St. Andrews. “However, this approach can impact animal welfare or be impossible to implement due to behavioural responses to anthropogenic factors or national/international legislation.” 

Indeed, I think that we can all agree that humans have stressed whales out enough as it is. Instead of invasive biopsies of skin and flesh with darts or scrapers, O’Mahony and his colleagues equipped drones with petri dishes and flew them through a total of 58 blows from 26 Northeast Pacific humpback whales in the Gitga'at First Nation territory of northern British Columbia.  

The team “established that a whole humpback whale genome can be recovered from exhaled respiratory vapour (‘blow’), marking a significant methodological advancement in non-invasive cetacean genomics.”

While it’s not the kind of blow most people associate with breathing orifices, it just might be what we need to study whales without hassling them.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins.
 
The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. 
"During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester.
 
"We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

items.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 

2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 
2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof 

Add a new headline to the list... 

2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries 

joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
 
[...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...]
 
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."
"If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone."
 
"If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
 
In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. 


But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports:


Just hours after Alpoge's claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. 
But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. 

"If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this," he wrote. "We are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere."

items.title: White House Withdraws Latest Nominee To Head The FDA; HHS Chaos Engine Goes Brrrrrr
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
I have said repeatedly that whatever else we can call RFK Jr.’s department of Health and Human Services, it is undoubtedly also a chaos engine. Between nominees who can’t get confirmed, vacant director level positions, other positions being filled by acting directors, and all the rest, HHS is currently producing confusion and incompetence more than anything else. We’ve also seen this at the FDA more specifically, with one chief regulator calling it quits after only three weeks, even though he himself was replacing another regulator who only made it a few months. Further up the chain, you’ll recall that Marty Makary only made it about a year as FDA commissioner before he quit.

In Makary’s place, Kyle Diamantas was named Acting Commissioner in May of this year. He’s still in that role today. The Federal Vacancies Reform Act limits an Acting Commissioner’s ability to serve in that role to 210 days. Diamantas is currently just shy of 200 days in his role to date. And, wouldn’t you know it, the White House has just withdrawn its nominee for FDA Commissioner for reasons nobody seems to totally understand.

The White House withdrew the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) amid opposition from Senate Republicans, it confirmed to The Hill.

Overton was set to face a key vote Wednesday in the Senate health committee, where Republicans hold only a one-vote majority — meaning losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.    

The White House said it was pulling the nomination because she didn’t have the votes needed to be confirmed. Strangely, the White House seems to be the only one that thinks that’s true. All that needed to happen was to placate a bunch of anti-abortion GOP senators, which seems like the lowest of hurdles over which the White House needed to leap. Here’s a guy who is routinely fooled by fake promises during confirmation hearings saying so out loud.

Cassidy said he was having “productive conversations” with committee members and believed Overton would have cleared his committee. The final hangup, he said, was anti-abortion senators seeking assurances from the administration about its commitment to “life issues.”

“My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk,” Cassidy wrote. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

That… doesn’t make a whole lot of sense. The Trump administration has never been shy about bowing to the anti-abortion wing of its own party. For her part, Overton is anti-abortion. She celebrated when Roe v. Wade was overturned. She refused in confirmation hearings when questioned to admit that mifepristone is medically safe.

This is starting to look instead like the MAHA movement is responsible for this and that it has nothing to do with abortion.

Former Kennedy senior adviser Calley Means, a prominent figure in the MAHA movement, said this month that Overton wrote a policy relaxing standards for fruit-flavored vapes.  

He also alleged Overton helped the Justice Department “construct a legal argument” for why the Supreme Court should take up a case that involved shielding major chemical company Bayer from lawsuits connected to its pesticide products. 

RFK Jr. recently stated that he now has the freedom to go full MAHA with Stephen Miller being named Chief of Staff. This smells for all the world like him, or other MAHA administration creeps, flexing this perceived new muscle and getting the Overton nomination pulled. That is rank speculation, of course, but it makes a great deal more sense than any concerns about abortion from Republican senators.

But, as Cassidy rightly stated, confirming the next FDA Commissioner will fall instead to a Congress controlled by Democrats. There will likely be another Acting Commissioner appointed, since Diamantas’ time will have run out. There won’t be time for new confirmation hearings.

The FDA, like it’s parent agency HHS, is once again outputting chaos.

An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says.
 
[...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. items.title: Tech Companies Are Trying To Shift The Entire Concept Of Privacy (Again)
items.author: Thorin Klosowski
items.content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. 

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. 

How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. 

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right?

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google’s blog post notes that it has whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. 

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. 

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. 

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. 

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: 

“And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. 

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

items.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

items.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

items.title: Judge Says DHS’s Seizure Of An Immigration Lawyer’s Phone Likely Violated The First Amendment
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
It’s logical to assume what happened here was a deliberate violation of immigration lawyer Andrew Lattarulo’s rights. The problem is that even deliberate violations need to be litigated. The ruling here paves the way for Lattarulo to continue his lawsuit against immigration officers who violated his rights. Unfortunately, winning here just generates another on-ramp to roads littered with insurmountable jurisprudence roadblocks.

But let’s not dwell on the potential futility of this lawsuit and instead dig into a decision where a federal judge has bucked the Supreme Court’s desire to excuse and all federal officers from accountability. This ruling finds in favor of someone whose rights were violated, rather than automatically assuming precedent demanded immediate dismissal. (h/t Kyle Cheney)

Early on in the decision [PDF], you can clearly see why immigration officers decided to engage in punitive action against Lattarulo. It’s not just that Lattarulo regularly defended people ICE wanted to make disappear, but he also actively informed other migrants of their rights via viral-esque videos:

Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents “thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings.” Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing “know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters,” [id. ¶ 59], which regularly “amasses hundreds of thousands of views…”

At some point, this lawyer and the law firm drew the attention of Trump’s anti-migrant forces. This led to normally unimaginable legal action by the Trump administration. The DHS’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit claimed the Cote law firm employed undocumented migrants. It demanded the firm turn over documentation on its employees — a demand the Cote law firm apparently complied with.

While HSI went through the motions of trying to find literally to shut down a law firm that provided zealous representation to detained migrants, Lattarulo and his employer decided to spend the weekend in Aruba. Cote returned from this trip and went through customs without incident.

Things went way worse for Lattarulo when he returned from the same weekend trip:

When his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

What’s on the record suggests the government did this not because it was essential to its border-securing work but simply because , given that it happened in one of the nation’s many constitutional dead zones, which not cover any international airport but anything up to 100 miles inland from any physical border crossing.

Supposedly, the government has not yet performed a search of the seized phone. But it definitely intends to… or at least believes it can work its way backwards from an unconstitutional search via any of the handy Get-Out-of-Lawsuit-Free cards the courts have provided it over the years.

The seized cell phone data is currently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits.

The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo’s clients.

So, there’s more than Lattarulo’s First Amendment rights at stake here. But if the government wants to engage in deliberate violations of attorney-client privilege, it first needs to convince a court that the seizure of Lattarulo’s phone has nothing to do with his immigration law work or his popular Instagram account that discusses these same legal issues.

Thus far, it’s not working out for the government. As the court notes in its discussion of the case, there is “no dispute” that Lattarulo’s public statements via his Instagram account (which include criticism of government policies and practices) are protected by the First Amendment. What needs to be demonstrated is that the seizure of the lawyer’s phone would likely not have happened if he hadn’t engaged in this criticism of the government.

This sure looks like illegal retaliation against this lawyer, says the Court. Before even getting to the matter of the phone seizure itself, the court points out that HSI aggressively accelerated its “investigation” of the law firm — trimming the response time for the firm to turn over documents from the stated ten days to , apparently for the sole reason of giving it a justification for the seizure of the lawyer’s phone upon his return to the United States.

Furthermore, if the government was truly interested in securing information from the law firm, rather than just looking for an excuse to seize an immigration lawyer’s phone, it would had detained the head of the law firm (Georges Cote) and demanded access to devices upon his arrival in the US a full day before Lattarulo’s plane landed. That HSI showed no interest in Cote — despite him being the ostensible target of its illegal employment investigation — makes it abundantly clear this was all about the government finding some way to punish Lattarulo for his speech and, possibly, illicitly gain access to his communications with ICE detainees.

The government asked the court to not only reject this lawsuit but to apply a “bright line” ruling stating that anything the government pretends to be “reasonable suspicion” is sufficient to excuse any resulting rights violations. The court says lol no, that won’t be happening.

Defendants seek a bright-line rule that because they had reasonable suspicion to conduct the search, Lattarulo cannot show that retaliation was a but-for cause. [Opp’n at 14–15]. The Court disagrees.

[T]he limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here and that Lattarulo’s own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property. The presence of reasonable suspicion therefore does not categorially bar a finding of causation under Nieves.

The court also addresses some of the Fourth Amendment concerns generated by HSI and ICE’s actions. While it’s not willing to rule on this issue (yet), mainly because these violations flow from the initial First Amendment violation, it doesn’t let them pass without comment.

The question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for “contraband” or for “evidence of contraband or a border-related crime.”

The difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at issue—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is “enforced or administered by CBP or ICE” but arguably is not a “border-related crime.” Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo’s border crossing (or, more broadly, the government’s interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government’s border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.

At the end of the day, the court finds in favor of the Constitution. Since the phone has already been returned to Lattarulo, the court doesn’t need to do much else other than forbid HSI from looking through the content it downloaded from the lawyer’s phone until further notice. Given what’s stated here, “further notice” will likely take the form of a ruling ordering the government to destroy the data it copied from the lawyer’s phone. If we’re lucky, the government will appeal this and end up creating even more precedent that works against it.

Until then, the government is on notice that this sort of stuff won’t fly, even when it’s happening in “Constitution-free zones” where a majority of US citizens reside, or — at the very least — pass through on a daily basis.

items.title: California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued subpoenas to Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang regarding reports that they misled investors about advanced AI chips potentially reaching China. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a press release. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information -- and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The probe follows Huang's resignation amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy and comes as the SEC reportedly conducts a similar investigation. The Hill reports: Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta continued.
 
[...] Following the Huang scandal, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents Thursday showing the U.S. authorized the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told The Hill, "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." "Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," the spokesperson added.

items.title: Wired Says ‘Please Let The Internet Die.’ Some Of Us Are Busy Building A Better One.
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
It remains incredible — and disturbing — to me how many people now think of the entire internet as being made up of a few giant enshittifying companies. I understand that is. The big companies absolutely do dominate much of the internet, and it’s close to impossible to avoid them entirely. But that doesn’t mean that that’s the entirety of the internet. And when you act as if it is, you do real damage to the good parts of the internet that still exist outside of the blast radius of those giants.

Five years ago, I wrote an article listing out a bunch of “other” internet websites, in the form of a “test suite” for anyone proposing internet regulations. Since most attempts to regulate the internet focus on the alleged (often not clearly proven) “harms” of one of the internet giants, I wanted people to think through the harm that these rules will do to the actual parts of the internet worth saving. These included forums and smaller shopping sites and web hosting and chat groups and more. It also included Wikipedia, which later picked up on the idea (I was told by someone there that this was partly inspired by my original article) and offered up “The Wikipedia Test.“

And yet, it seems difficult for people to remember this. It’s just so to bitch and moan that the internet now is just Meta and Google and Amazon and TikTok and (these days) OpenAI or whatever. And it leads to silly articles like Wired’s recent article Please Let the Internet Die.

But if you read through it, the entire article is about enshittifying internet giants, with the assumption that because all suck, the rest of the internet should die as well.

It is ridiculous to conclude that because some giant parts of the internet are enshittifying, there’s little worth saving in the rest of it. But that’s exactly where this article lands.

To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn outbad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs haveto such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by

In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

You can open up any of those links in the last two sentences and read about the excitement and the building, but I’ll just grab a bit from that last link:

The open web of the nineties didn’t win because the tools were better. It won because a critical mass of people decided that the alternative, a handful of AOL-style walled gardens choosing what everyone saw, was not the future they wanted. Then they built their way out of it. Slowly, unglamorously, in rooms that looked a lot like this one.

Whether atproto ends up being the thing, or a stepping stone to the thing, I don’t know. Nobody in the room claimed to know. But the work is real, the apps are shipping, and the people building them are taking it seriously without taking themselves seriously. That combination is rare, and historically, it’s the one that wins.

But if people just accept that “the internet needs to die,” we don’t get there. We get more stupid regulations that lock in those enshittifying giants and make it impossible to build a better internet.

The Wired piece is, in theory, a review of a new book called “The Internet Will Die,” which, at least as Wired presents it, frames the internet as fragile and doomed to cycles of decay, with big companies making things worse and deleting our digital histories along the way:

For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.

If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in alosing arms race for attentionwith low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.

But, again, that assumes an internet dominated by a handful of giants, the ones you hand all your data to, is the only internet possible.

But we already know that’s not true and it doesn’t need to be true in the future either. It sounds like West’s framing in his book is to encourage users to be more thoughtful about where they spend their time and energy online — and that’s great — but as Wired frames it, it’s all a wasteful endeavor since it’s always going to suck.

I certainly understand the fatalistic feeling that the internet sucks and will continue to suck. But that’s only true for people who lock themselves into the environments controlled by the internet giants you hate, rather than getting out and looking around at the cool things people are building which put the users in control of their own experience.

The piece ends with the author of the article, Miles Klee, admitting that the author of the book, John West, at least is open to the idea that a better internet can be created. But Klee, a self-described failed composter who’s “too lazy” for the gross work involved, doubts enough people will ever bother to do it.

“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.

And, again, I get the attitude, but I find this self-defeating nihilism to be pointless. The entire point of the internet, as Konstantinos Komaitis reminded us recently, is that it is . The internet is built on protocols that let anyone come in and build something better. Deciding we should just give up because some of the biggest players now suck is letting enshittification win.

The seeds of a better internet have already been planted. You can join Klee and Wired in doubting that enough gardeners will show up, but plenty of people are already out there digging. Come join us!

items.title: Tesla Starts ‘Selling’ Cybercabs You Can’t Buy With A $299/Month Automation Fee In Latest Ploy
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Instead, Musk envisions pivoting Tesla so it focuses more on AI and automation — despite the fact that the company’s AI systems aren’t profitable or particularly popular amidst a sea of better options, and many of Musk’s robotics and automation efforts mostly consist of hype, vaporware, or stuff that will never really see a mass commercial launch (like the nonexistent Optimum robot).

Speaking of hype, Tesla recently took to Elon Musk’s right wing propaganda website to announce that the company would soon be “selling” Cybercabs to consumers. According to the announcement, the Cybercab is being sold for $29,990 (before taxes and insurance). Plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription” charge:

Of course with everything Musk, the actual details matter. It’s invite only, meaning you won’t get one. Indeed it’s pretty clear that most people won’t actually be able to buy one. The car is only allowed to drive in a few cities (mainly, Austin, Texas), so you probably wouldn’t be able to actually drive the vehicle if you were actually able to buy one (which you won’t). And even if you happen to live in one of the zones where it currently can drive, you can’t leave those zones.

And the fine print indicates that on the off chance you actually get one (again, you won’t), you won’t be able to put the car to work as an automated taxi, despite Musk and Tesla’s earlier promises on this front:

“One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car.”

That $299 per month fee adds an additional $17,940 to the vehicle sticker price over five years. And the fine print indicates that Tesla reserves the right to charge you even more for automation, provided they give you a 30 day advanced warning. So the rich layers of bullshit are all .

There’s also the fact that these vehicles likely aren’t going to be very safe as the company conducts a glorified alpha test on public streets. Musk’s legendary decision to overrule his engineers on radar/lidar and go camera only for self-driving has already resulted in no shortage of human deaths. Meanwhile America’s safety regulators have been too corrupt, captured, or feckless to do anything about.

While Tesla’s CFO insists the company wants to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation,” there’s very little indication that the company has the chops to fend off competitors and dominate the space. Most of what Musk now does is designed to prop up his fake supergenius engineer mythology, despite the ratio of bullshit to actual innovation becoming more and more lopsided.

So to prop up that mythology and goose comically inflated stock valuations, Musk is clearly keen on bundling and conflating Tesla’s increasingly stale vehicle lineup and “me too” automation and AI efforts with SpaceX’s actually innovative launch and Starlink technologies, and hoping the lion’s share of the press and public isn’t bright enough to notice the AI and automation stuff is .

You can expect a Tesla and SpaceX merger in 2027 specifically for this reason.

It continues to say nothing good about America (or our media) how easily Elon Musk convinced the press and public he was a supergenius engineer who could cobble together complicated rocket machinery wearing coveralls in his backyard shed.
