items.title: Amazon Fights the Delivery Protection Act With Homepage Banner, In-App Pop-Up
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I'm met with a vertical banner that reads: "ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order" with a button that says "Act now." The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon.
 
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses. Clicking on "Act now" on Amazon's homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states: "Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The move marks an unusual expansion of Amazon's political advocacy, reports Ars, and raises concerns about the company's ability to influence shoppers and present a one-sided view of legislation.
 
The bill, which also affects companies like FedEx and DoorDash, remains stalled in a City Council committee, with no vote scheduled.

items.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
items.author: Jacob Hoffman-Andrews
items.content:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?

Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.

One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.

While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (or to malicious hackers), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.

Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.

Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.

This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decisionmakers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.

This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.

When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of debtissues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues.

What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written.

For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once.

Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security.

For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company.

Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud.

Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical  to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable.

items.title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
items.author: Joe Mullin
items.content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology.

That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong.

Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard.

Petitions and Institution Rates Are Falling

Since Congress created the IPR patent challenge process in 2012, the PTAB has always had some discretion in deciding which petitions deserve review. But institution rates today are much lower than their typical historical range.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, the PTAB instituted between 66% and 68% of IPR petitions. In fiscal year 2026, which concluded in September 2026, the institution rate fell to 41%. And institution is only the first step of an IPR—it means the PTAB has agreed to hear the challenge, not that the challenger won, and the patent will be invalidated.

That decline helps explain why fewer petitions are being filed in the first place. Preparing an IPR petition takes substantial time and money. While cheaper than federal court, it’s still a complicated administrative process. Before filing, a challenger typically needs to search for prior art, hire experts, and develop detailed technical and legal arguments about why the patent never should have been granted.

Companies were willing to pay for IPRs because, historically, they could expect a predictable process. Petitions that met the statutory standard generally had a reasonable prospect of being heard and decided on the merits. But the USPTO has made it harder to get petitions heard and is throwing them out for reasons that have nothing to do with the merits of the challenges. Faced with these odds, many potential challengers aren’t filing at all.

Even After a Challenge Is Accepted, The USPTO Director Can Cancel It

When the PTAB decides to hear an IPR case, that means the petition has been “instituted”—but that has never meant that the petitioner will definitely win. It means the PTAB has determined the challenge warrants a full merits review, and the parties could expect the proceeding to continue toward a final written decision. But under the current USPTO leadership, that expectation has disappeared. The PTAB’s institution decisions are being repeatedly vacated by the Director.

USPTO Director John Squires has vacated at least 29 decisions granting institution of IPR proceedings, and subsequently denied the petitions, terminating those proceedings before a final written decision. These include cases that PTAB judges had already agreed to hear, as well as proceedings that Squires himself had previously allowed to proceed. This level of retroactive intervention is unprecedented.

In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution.

For example, in Revvo Technologies v. Cerebrum Sensor Technologies, the Director vacated an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the Director reversed that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings.

The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work.

Congress Created the PTAB To Avoid Costly Litigation

Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes.

That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology.

EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don’t just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target small businesses and independent developers, and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control.

If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge.

We Shouldn’t Accept This as the New Normal

Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits.

These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don’t bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing.

If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won’t stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation.

items.title: Court Tells Cops That The 4th Amendment Doesn’t Cover AI-Generated ‘Probable Cause’
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
I don’t know where this decision will take us, but its implications reach much further than the single case it covers. AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports.

In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department.

The detective decided to run a screenshot of the suspect’s face (derived from the CCTV footage) through the PD’s facial recognition program. The decision [PDF] doesn’t specify which facial recognition program was used, but given that the match was made using photos found on Facebook, it suggests Clearview AI might have been involved, given its scraping of hundreds of billions of images from the open web since its inception.

Not that it did anything useful in terms of actual detective work. Nor did it do anything remotely constitutional, not when the operative word in “probable cause” is “probable.”

Relying solely on the AI identification, Detective Kilmer concluded that the match was accurate. [Id. at 4–5]. The Facebook profile belonged to an individual known as “Yony Smith Npoles Charon,” and for an unknown reason, Detective Kilmer concluded that “Yony” was actually Alain Vizcay Osorio—the man in the booking photo.

The court says “for an unknown reason.” I can make an educated guess, however. Passing a bad check is the sort of crime most cops won’t really dig into. Detective Kilmer was handed the case and did the bare minimum: he ran an AI-assisted search. He didn’t actually do anything that resembled detective work. But he still felt his 30 seconds of non-existent effort were enough to support a criminal complaint and the issuance of an arrest warrant.

Osorio — who lived in — was arrested and extradited to to face criminal charges. He was released on bond the day after his arrest (January 24, 2025). He was then indicted by a grand jury in March 2025 and arraigned roughly two months later. Again, Osorio pleaded not guilty. At that point, the state’s attorney’s office dismissed the charges after Osorio provided proof he had been working in Nebraska at the time the bad check was being passed by (the presumably still at-large) suspect captured by the bank’s security camera.

The only thing the AI used by the detective seemed to be capable of doing was reinforcing the investigator’s “all Black people look the same” prejudices. (To be clear, I don’t specifically know if this detective has these prejudices, but the chain of events in this case certainly support an assumption of this person’s assumptions, if you catch my drift.)

The individuals in the security footage and the Facebook profile image do not resemble the booking photo of Osorio. [Id. at 6–7]. Based on the booking photo, the only thing Osorio has in common with the suspect is that he is a black male with facial hair. [Dkt. 3-1 at 2–3]. Based on the photographs, it appears that Osorio has a different head shape, different haircut, different facial features, and different complexion.

Detective Kilmer told the court (via his affidavit) that he had used “investigative tools” to “match” Osario to the suspect. In reality, the court says, Kilmer only used a tool and rolled with its obviously faulty conclusions despite Florence PD policy stating facial recognition AI alone is not enough to “establish probable cause.”

Kilmer runs directly into this policy and the Fourth Amendment itself, which poses multiple problems for his desire to walk away fiscally intact from this lawsuit. The policy is undeniable, which means Kilmer deliberately ignored his “training” and any “expertise” it was supposed to impart.

But beyond that, there’s the Fourth Amendment itself, which can’t as easily be ignored as cop shop software clickwrap. That much is made perfectly clear in the court’s introductory paragraph:

The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause. In other words, the Fourth Amendment does not permit an individual to be arrested based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual in question has committed a crime. And no reasonable detective in the Defendant’s position could conclude otherwise.

The first part of that suggests implications far beyond this case, given how often “detectives” are letting their fingers do the walking (so to speak) and pretending whatever the computer coughs up is arrest-worthy. That’s not just the facial recognition tech used in this case. This is also the AI that steers patrols and public interactions via so-called “predictive policing.” That’s also the AI that writes reports for police officers, allowing the computer to create the permanent, official record of stops, arrests, and uses of force.

But what’s also important is the last sentence of that paragraph. That’s the thing that’s going to make this stick. The detective isn’t shielded by qualified immunity, which means this is sure to be appealed. But if this officer does this (rather than “allow” the people who he’s supposed to be serving to buy him out of a lawsuit via a settlement), he’s going to make this an appellate case. And there’s definitely no reason to assume the higher court is just going to blow off the obvious concerns raised by this lawsuit and allow QI to cover up this compendium of wrongs.

For now, the decision stands as it is: AI isn’t probable cause. Never has been. Never should be. And if this court has anything to say about it, it never be. Detectives who prefer to let computers do their thinking for them might want to dial back their reliance on algorithms. Justice should never be subject to available processing power. And if you lack the desire (or intelligence!) to do detective work properly, well…

items.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
 
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.

items.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say

items.content:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

items.title: Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.
 
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
 
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

items.title: ICE Adds A New Layer Of Cruelty By Deliberately Hiding The Current Locations Of Detained Migrants
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
No one in this administration is worth saving. You could just put them all on a boat and sink it in a ocean and only the publisher still waiting to recoup the advance on a “Hillbilly Elegy” sequel will shed any tears.

The administration got its ass kicked in the mid-terms. And while Trump had very little coherence to offer while it was happening, he’s back in the driver’s seat again. For now. The ghoul traveling in Trump’s orbit has been elevated to Chief of Staff. Stephen Miller — who actively embodies the Nazi-ism he wants to see in the world — has even more power, now that he’s officially a high-ranking staff member.

The rest of the administration is similarly under pressure to produce results, especially now that at the stroke of Midnight 2027, it will no longer control the House the Senate. While this latest update on administration awfulness predates the mid-terms (but just barely), rest assured it will be amplified, abused, and otherwise exploited to ensure maximum evil until it becomes something the government seeks to rein in, rather than simply something the Trump administration can deploy without fear of reprisal.

There are lots of things we already know about Trump’s mass deportation program. First and foremost, it has nothing to do with removing dangerous migrants from the US. Its entire purpose is to rid this country of “others” — brown or black people who aren’t nearly as white as they should be. Where they end up matters not at all. It only matters that they’re gone.

The administration has allies in places it definitely shouldn’t have allies. The Fifth Circuit has been an absolute outlier since Trump’s return to office, rejecting thousands of federal court rulings to the contrary across the nation to declare migrants have no due process rights. This runs contrary to the Constitution and 10,000+ court rulings but it doesn’t really matter. Texas and Louisiana have massive ICE detention facilities. And detainees are swiftly routed to this jurisdiction to ensure they’re deprived of their rights until the government decides which random hellhole it wants to send them to.

The judicial system continues to catch the government in the act of depriving right. And the government continues to insist it doesn’t matter what the system of checks and balances has to say about its actions. There’s a lot of friction and it’s not going to go away, not matter how many unlawful executive orders are issued.

But there’s still this Fifth Circuit pressure valve, which currently allows the government to speedily shift detainees to detention centers where their rights aren’t respected. And this is on top of the normal bullshit pulled by ICE et al, where the constant movement of detainees is a deliberate effort to deprive them of their due process rights by keeping jurisdiction in constant flux.

Now there’s a new wrinkle: one that’s meant to be more of the same. And it’s also something no other administration has attempted prior to this point in history. This is brute force rights removal, performed by an administration that would rather see you bankrupted than rein in any of its ugliest urges:

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders, an unannounced move that has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice.

ICE removed those detainees from its online detainee locator system on Sept. 15, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the change. Several lawyers contacted by The Associated Press confirmed their clients vanished from the system this week, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association warned its members about the situation Friday.

Plenty of administrations have lied and cheated. But this is the only administration that has openly declared it would rather cheat than play fairly and has still somehow managed to retain most of its power even though thousands of courts have not only called out its cheating, but restored rights to thousands of people the administration has indiscriminately subjected to its very specific forms of discrimination.

Where it goes from here is unknown. Courts can issue orders that will try to return the status to quo. But it’s unlikely any of this will matter until MAGA becomes a minority group itself. Without the full-throated cowardice of the Republic Party to back whatever play Trump (or Stephen Miller) chooses to make, what’s seen here — as awful as it is — might be the beginning of the end.

Unfortunately for those swept up ICE raids, these disappearances will still be effective enough to see them deprived of their rights, if not actually deported to countries more than willing to let foreigners die on their soil so long it results in a paycheck or, perhaps, a bit more respect from a country that has chosen to turn its back on its human rights record.

items.title: Oh Sure, NOW Nick Clegg Tells Tech Bros They Were Wrong To Back Trump
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
I’m getting a bit tired of the so-called “prodigal tech bros” who worked in tech companies, and only really speak out about the terrible decisions made by the leaders of those companies after they leave (at which point they get way more press coverage than anyone who has been criticizing those decisions all along). But this new piece from Nick Clegg in The Atlantic, saying that “Getting Too Close to Trump Was a Mistake“, feels like a new variation on the genre. Like the prodigal tech bros, his message isn’t necessarily wrong, just coming way too late from a messenger who should have actually taken a stand earlier.

If you don’t recall, Nick Clegg is the former UK politician (and deputy Prime Minister) who then went to Facebook/Meta, where he spent a few years as their “President for Global Affairs” (effectively, second in command to Zuck) where he tended to be rolled out to take political heat for unpopular decisions. He was the one who made it clear that Zuck was willing to give up Section 230 to allow governments to “regulate” Facebook… in a manner that would harm Meta’s competitors way more than Meta.

He left in January of 2025 as Trump’s second term was set to begin, allowing Joel Kaplan — who was way more connected to US GOP politics — to take his place. So, in some sense, it’s little surprise that Clegg is now willing to throw Trump under the bus. But also, a bit late for that, Nick. Some of us were calling this shit out right away, when it was still extremely politically inconvenient to do so, rather than waiting until after the American public spoke out loud and clear during the midterms.

As for Clegg’s reasoning as to why Silicon Valley’s leaders lined up behind Trump, he’s right that they basically got none of what they hoped to get:

First, tech leaders said that uniting the power of Washington and Silicon Valley would help America in its fight with China for AI supremacy. Yet over the past 18 months, China has been closing the gap with the United States by most objective measures, including model performance and chip development. In some important respects, China has outpaced America altogether, deploying open-weight models faster, developing a more sustainable energy strategy, and training world-class researchers and engineers at a larger scale.

Second, Silicon Valley leaders said that partnering with the government would help assuage public concerns about AI and overcome the “woke” opposition to Big Tech. Yet societal attitudes toward AI in the U.S. are much more negative now than they ever were under President Biden, and worse than almost anywhere else on the planet. Fostering the very backlash they claimed they were trying to confront is a peculiar triumph of hubris and incompetence.

Third, tech executives hoped that earning Trump’s good graces would allow them to avoid unwelcome regulatory incursions outside the U.S., especially in Europe. The Trump administration has undoubtedly helped with this in some ways. For example, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has become an important ally for tech leaders trying to fight a number of European Union enforcement decisions. But by any other meaningful measure the approach has been a disaster: Anti–Big Tech, and (alas) anti-American, sentiment has never been higher in large parts of the world, and most major economies—including Canada’s, India’s, Germany’s, and Brazil’s—are now scrambling to have less, not more, of what Silicon Valley produces.

Since Silicon Valley pivoted to Trump, then, its scorecard has looked something like this:chief rival (China) strengthened; domestic support weakened; global markets infuriated.

Again, though, there were plenty of people who warned about this as soon as they started up lining up behind Trump (even before the 2024 election). None of this was difficult to predict. So it seems a bit unseemly to bring all this up now.

Clegg’s analysis of they missed it so much is at least a little bit more interesting. I’m not sure I agree with them all. His first one is that they had “FOMO” about Elon Musk’s close relationship with Trump, and were worried that this would undercut their own company’s efforts while competing with Musk’s companies. I don’t buy that FOMO alone explains it — the miscalculation seems so obvious that almost anyone could have seen it coming from the start.

The more interesting one to me is this one:

. Tech leaders had a lot to be angry about in the run-up to Trump’s reelection. Some felt unfairly treated by traditional media, academia, and cultural elites. Conservatives had long felt unwelcome in the Valley’s traditionally liberal milieu. The Biden administration had clumsily vilified tech leaders rather than work with them on policy and regulation. These factors created a large group of powerful, wealthy, and offended individuals. Stepping into the Trump tent seemed like a good way to even the score.

I actually do think this was a major motivating factor among many (and have pointed that out a few times as well). But Clegg should point out how pathetic and silly this is. Tech leaders are some of the most powerful executives in the world. The fact that they got so offended that the Biden admin didn’t kiss their ass is no reason to throw in with fascism. This has nothing to do with high school popularity and cliques — it’s about having some fucking standards about humanity and basic rights.

On the next point, though, I do think Clegg is spot on:

Misunderstanding politics. As someone who spent nearly two decades in elected office and has spent much of my time since working in and around tech, I am always struck by how eagerly smart and wealthy people expound on subjects about which they know very little—especially politics. Their commercial success seems to foster in them a view that politics is easy, if only dim-witted officeholders would listen to them. It is this hubris that makes the Valley such an exhilarating and exasperating place.

I don’t think this is necessarily limited to tech bros. Indeed, I don’t think it’s necessarily limited to the wealthy. Lots of people have very strong (often ill-informed) opinions on lots of things. The real problem is that with the ultra wealthy, people feel a ridiculous obligation to take their brain farts on other subjects seriously. That’s where the mistakes come in. This is compounded by the assumption that because tech bros create magical-seeming innovations, they must also have special insight into policy and the future. I’m as critical as anyone of politicians not understanding tech, but the same is true in the other direction, where people in tech tend to have a very confused and unrealistic understanding of politics.

But a big part of the problem is that people take the stupid policy ideas from the tech bros seriously because of their wealth and the fact that they once lucked into selling some random business for hundreds of millions of dollars. And it seems like many of the tech bros assumed — incorrectly — that the public adulation they had received for years for their innovations would follow them into the realm of politics.

The reality is the reverse has happened. As they’ve embraced fascism and Trumpism, rather than having the public come along with them, the public (especially younger people) no longer trust them at all. Embracing Trumpism completely burned bridges with young Americans:

But again, this turn of events shouldn’t have been a surprise. Innovators were celebrated when they focused on making people’s lives better, and actually empowering them. But over the last decade, the leaders of the field, the same ones who lined up behind Donald Trump, seemed to totally ignore how the public’s views regarding their own platforms had shifted. And that’s because they had shifted from an era of actually empowering people to one of extracting as much as they could from them, and then demanding more.

The innovations no longer seemed cool and interesting and empowering. They seemed needy and aggressive and extractive.

Clegg’s piece is frustrating in that there are elements of it that are absolutely accurate. But it comes way too late and in too weak a form. As I said right after the election, much of Silicon Valley is actually working on unique and useful innovations and doesn’t support the fascist MAGA project. But too many of the CEOs and the VCs decided to buy in, and now they’re going to face blowback. My fear is that the blowback directed at the shitty leaders of shitty companies will actually do more damage to the underlying internet that people still rely on, rather than just narrowly targeting the actual bad actors.

While Clegg admits that Democrats in Congress are likely to investigate the tech industry for their coziness with Trump, he misses the larger point: the blast radius of those investigations will go beyond just those companies that embraced what they thought was a fascist cheat code to dominance. It’s going to make it much harder for the actual innovation, the smaller companies, and the new services that actually empower people, to exist as well. The end result is going to be a lockdown on the wider industry, because a few shithead leaders of the biggest companies couldn’t think just a few steps into the future.

There’s real collateral damage from the tech bros’ embrace of fascism, and avoiding it starts with not sugarcoating what a mess this was all along — and discussing directly how much damage their embrace of Trumpist fascism will do to the good parts of the internet.

items.title: Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels.
 
Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

items.title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.

Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.

“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”

AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.

“Adding to the chorus of people who sold an item thru AptDeco and never received payment. I have no idea what to do at this point,” another says. 

“Can we do a class action lawsuit?” another reads.

“They owed me money since September 30th,” a fourth says. 

Every recent review and complaint on AptDeco’s Better Business Bureau page is from sellers who have not been paid: “Almost 6 weeks after they picked up and not being paid Pick up was a nightmare too No calls nobody doing anything Do NOT SELL ON APTDECO,” one reads. Another states “I have been in an endless loop with customer service for 2 months trying to get my payout for the bed I sold. I am losing faith that I will ever see this money. Extremely frustrated at this experience.”

On AptDeco’s website, everything appears to be business as usual. You can still buy and sell furniture, and there is no indication of anything wrong at all. 404 Media’s repeated attempts to reach AptDeco to ask what was going on went unreturned.

In communications with sellers seen by 404 Media, AptDeco’s customer service representatives have repeatedly blamed their payment processor, a “technical bug,” or have said the payment is “moving through the system.” On November 3, AptDeco told Erin that a bug had prevented her from being paid, that the payment team “retried” it, and that she would be paid within 10 days. 

“I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally, so you should see it in your bank account by then - hopefully sooner! At this point, we’re doing everything we can to get your payout processed,” a customer support email reviewed by 404 Media reads. On Tuesday, two weeks after the company told her the payment had been retried, a different customer service representative followed up and said “I'm truly sorry — I know this isn't the update you were hoping for. Your payout is still being prioritized by our payments team, and I want to be honest with you: I don't yet have a confirmed release date or timeline to share.”

Several other people who have sold items on AptDeco recently told 404 Media they’re experiencing the same problem.

Harry Heymann sold a Room & Board couch on AptDeco in late September and still has not been paid the $120 he is owed by the platform. The messages he’s gotten from AptDeco customer support read much the same as Erin’s: They claim “a technical bug on our end held up your payout” and the customer service representative said “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally.” Late last week, he got what reads like an AI-generated message that reads “I know how frustrating this has been. You've been waiting on your $120 payout, the date you were given has passed, and you've had to follow up to get answers. That's not the experience we want for you, and I'm truly sorry. Your case has been escalated to me, and l'm happy to be your point of contact from here. Unfortunately, the issue with our payment processor has not yet been resolved, and our team is still working on it.” 

Natalie Simmons sold an armoire in late August and told 404 Media she initially had a good experience compared to using other platforms. But then she never got her money. 

“After so many uncomfortable situations on different social sites I was so happy when I found AptDeco,” she told me. “I received notification that my payment would arrive in 3-5 business days through the portal in app. That was Aug 30th. I tried calling but the voicemail says leave a message and they will respond by email. I emailed several times and finally after 2 weeks and a few voicemails I received an email that there was a glitch with their payment system and I will receive payment within 5-10 business days. After another 2 weeks I called and emailed again that I still didn’t receive payment. They sent another email with the exact same story. I just want to get paid. It’s not even that much but it’s the principle.”

It’s not just sellers who have had issues with the platform. One customer, K Turner, bought a couch and tried to return it. Rather than giving her a refund, the company said they would relist it at the price she paid and then give her a “refund” of whatever it sold for minus fees. The couch resold quickly at the beginning of September and the company told her she would quickly get her “refund.” More than a month later, on October 20, they told her “I have gone ahead and processed that refund ($600) manually. Please allow 5-10 business days for this refund to be reflected back to your original form of payment.” She has still not gotten her money. 

“The communication was decent at first, but once they confirmed the item resold on September 8th, they then went silent. It took me a month to finally get a response. They confirmed that the item resold at the full listing price of $600 and that I would receive my refund to my original payment in 5 - 10 business days,” Turner told me. “That was nearly a month ago, and I still don't have my money. So, they effectively double-dipped. They got my money from the original order and then collected money by reselling it. And who knows if they ever gave the money to the original seller; maybe they triple-dipped. I have threatened legal action twice now.”

The customers I spoke to have no idea what happens next. Some of them said they were going to file claims in small claims court or are considering a class action lawsuit. But the company is mostly giving them what appear to be canned, copy-pasted statements that come from a revolving cast of customer support email addresses, and no actual updates. Four emails from 404 Media asking for comment, including emails sent to the company’s CEO, have not been returned. AptDeco promises a high-end, safe experience when compared to somewhere like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, and markets itself primarily for more expensive, lightly-used furniture. The people I spoke to said they wish they had just stayed off the platform altogether.

“The irony is that I’m now feeling safer selling expensive designer furniture directly to strangers on Facebook Marketplace than through a platform whose entire purpose is supposedly to make these transactions safer and more secure,” Erin said. “At this point, AptDeco has my furniture, I have no money, and I’m left chasing them for something I’m already owed. It’s an incredibly unsettling position to be in, particularly when so many other sellers seem to be experiencing the same thing. The fact that I continue to receive email marketing newsletters and see them selling via Google Ads—paying that platform before their sellers—is infuriating.”

After this article was published (and three days after we initially asked for comment), an AptDeco spokesperson gave 404 Media a convoluted explanation involving “bot swarms,” which it blamed for the delays in seller payouts. “Over the past few months, we’ve been dealing with an unprecedented volume of bot activity, some of it malicious. This has created a myriad of challenges that we’ve been actively working to address.These bot swarms, along with the broader cybersecurity challenges of an AI-evolving world, prompted us to significantly strengthen our site’s security to ensure the long-term protection of our buyers and sellers,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear, customer data has not been compromised in any way. However, we’ve been investing heavily in preventative measures to further protect our community. Unfortunately, some of these efforts have resulted in delays in seller payouts.  As you can imagine, cybersecurity is a complex and sensitive topic, making it challenging to communicate all the details broadly. That said, the issue has now been resolved, and outstanding payouts are being processed. Any seller with questions can email and will hear back within 1 business day. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”

When I asked for clarification because it was not clear how bot swarms would affect payouts, the spokesperson said “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.”

“We deployed code to further improve protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing. Providing additional technical context would require a detailed understanding of our codebase and would likely be more information than is relevant or useful to readers,” they added. “That said, we sincerely apologize to our customers for the delays and are committed to making things right. The issue has been resolved, our security infrastructure remains extremely robust, and outstanding payouts are being processed. We appreciate you reaching out and giving us the opportunity to clarify. This will be our final comment on the matter.”

items.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.

According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers ran the numbers by examining 81,000 US census tracts and location data for 5,291 data centers. “We found that these racial disparities persist even after accounting for factors such as population, household income, education, land costs, proximity to major transmission lines, and state fixed effects,” they wrote. “These results hold even though data centers are concentrated in and around metropolitan areas, which are often more racially diverse.”

“We really wanted to look at this on a nationwide scale to see: is this something that fits into this broader structural racism story?” CSINT executive director Samantha Bradshaw told 404 Media. “What we did find was yes [...] neighborhoods that have data centers tend to have a higher ratio of people of color.”

Bradshaw and co-author Dhanaraj Thakur told 404 Media that they were inspired to do the study after reading stories about data centers in Memphis, Tennessee polluting Black and Brown communities. Another high profile case occurred in Taylor, Texas where a white family donated a tract of land to the city with the intention it become a public part. That land abutted a Black neighborhood. The city never built a park there and now it’s slated to become a data center

According to the researchers, the historical legacy of — the process of denying Americans of color loans and other opportunities to keep them in specific neighborhoods — is to blame for some of this. Data centers are often built near transmission lines because they provide ease of access to power infrastructure, for example. Those transmission lines were often built in majority Black neighborhoods in America. 

Thakur said he doubted that data centers developers were seeking to intentionally put data centers in communities of color. “It’s just how embedded race is with all these other factors,” he said. 

The study distinguished between several different kinds of data centers and noted there are massive differences between hyperscalers like what Meta, Google, and Grok are building and smaller mixed use buildings that often serve as network transmission hubs as well as compute warehouses, which the study called “co-location facilities.” When a hyperscaler comes to town, the developers sometimes promise economic investment in the community where it’s being constructed and those facilities typically aren’t built in communities of color..

Meta is building a $50 billion data center in rural Louisiana. Community leaders there have said it would bring 1,000 permanent jobs and that sales tax revenues have already jumped 2,000 percent, leading to a $50,000 bonus for area teachers. Even here, there is disparity. Most of the hyperscalers that promise massive economic benefits to local communities are built in white rural communities. 

The study makes several suggestions about what to do about all this including data center-specific zoning regulations, prioritizing racial equity in discussions around building them, and requiring racial impact statements for data centers before they’re built. 

Thakur and Bradshaw emphasized that tech policy should be a negotiation between the companies that provide the tech and the communities that use it. Data centers have spurred these conversations — they’re physical representations of Big Tech’s powers, a power that Americans recently rejected at the ballot box. “AI has a physical geography, and that geography is shaped by political and social history,” the researchers wrote in the study.

“I think the issue around how racial justice, civil rights plays into many other kinds of policies —health, education, housing, whatever it is — we just don't see enough of that consideration in tech policy, and I think this this kind of analysis shows why this that why we should be doing that, thinking about that more,” Thakur said.

Bradshaw agreed. “If you look at who's represented in tech policy and who built these systems, who designs them, who engineers them, it's a very specific kind of white male Silicon Valley California ideology engineer, and that is not representative of the technology and its users,” she said. “So I think bringing in these perspectives is really really important because then we can truly think about ways to design a tech future that is for everybody.

items.title: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
This article was primarily reported using public records requests. We are making it available to all readers as a public service. FOIA reporting can be expensive, please consider subscribing to 404 Media to support this work. Or send us a one time donation via our tip jar here.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. 

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.

Do you know anything else about this data? Do you work at ICE or another federal agency using it? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.

items.title: Nvidia And The Trump Administration Begin ‘Investigating’ Themselves In Wake Of Blossoming Scandal
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
As is always the case with this sort of stuff, the scandal is likely to get much worse. And the multiple, overlapping looming investigations (including several of the congressional variety) aren’t likely to restrict themselves simply to extramarital affairs and the alleged Chinese spy.

That’s causing a lot of panic in the AI sector that the hugely profitable GPU monopoly will stop massively subsidizing numerous unprofitable AI companies, exposing the circular, dodgy financing propping up the entire industry. As a result there was a short-lived manufactured effort by guys like Elon Musk and David Sacks over the weekend to demonize the journalists behind the story, frame the whole thing as a conspiracy, and have Huang reinstated before the check comes due for their funny financial math.

The Nvidia board has made it clear they’re not willing to take that risk and put Huang back in place before they know the full scope of what Huang was up to. It would be legal suicide to do otherwise. Huang, for his part, issued a statement saying that he had spent a few days atoning for multiple affairs and potential national security violations, and was ready to get back to work!

You’ll notice the same treatment over at Semafor, which informs us that the Trump DOJ antitrust division has launched an “investigation” into Nvidia (which again, would never have this amount of linchpin power in a country with functional antitrust enforcement):

“One of those probes, on antitrust grounds, is focused specifically on the chipmaker, these people say, while two other inquiries focus on tech companies Megaspeed and Supermicro. The Megaspeed and Supermicro probes have focused on the involvement of Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy that Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with before he resigned. There’s no indication that the DOJ would seek to charge Nvidia, or Huang, criminally at this time.”

The stories reflect at worst a complicity, and at best a strange normalization bias among U.S. journalists, who feel compelled to pretend that U.S. regulators still function in the public interest and haven’t been hollowed out like a cheap Dollar Store chocolate Easter bunny by Trumpism. It clashes strangely with the quality journalism at major outlets that exposed the scandal in the first place.

Hopefully Democrats don’t fuck this up. But you definitely get the sense there are a lot more sordid details to come, with multiple, massive overlapping implications for everyone in the new year.

items.title: Charting American Culture in News Footage of ‘Grand Theft Auto’
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Some people spent the week leading up to the release of replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years.

Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI.

For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. GTA is the American id made manifest.

You can chart America’s changing culture — especially its anxieties — by watching how the media covered Grand Theft Auto. This was, at first, the game that critics of the medium had always warned us about: a violent sex and death simulator that rotted the brains of the youth just as rock and roll and comics had done in ages past. Twenty years on, the brains are thoroughly rotted, GTA won, and now? Now we’re all worried about money.

GTA III and — Murder Simulators, the Assassin of Youth

Rockstar released in October 2001 and just a year later. The controversy around both started right away and centered around violence, and sometimes, the game’s depiction of women. “This is the world’s most popular video game [...] and millions of kids are mastering it by learning to slaughter bystanders,” Ted Koppel told America.

Nightline devoted 20 minutes of its broadcast to GTA in July 2002. It interviewed children who grinned ear to ear as they gunned down people in GTA, their parents who insisted it was just a game, a concerned expert who was sure GTA was training them to kill, and a psychologist who said that was bullshit. It all ended with a roundtable discussion where a police officer, in uniform, explained the differences between video games and real world violence.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas — Congressional Hearings and Sex on TV

I was an assistant manager of a Gamestop in Texas in 2004 when Rockstar released Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. The level of parental concern in the store was high in the weeks leading up to its release. One mother was so upset by a bearing a cover story about that she told me I was going to hell for “selling a gangster lifestyle” to children.

But it was sex, not violence, that the news focused on with . The game had a lot of simulation elements — its protagonist would gain weight if he ate too much — and Rockstar had experimented with a sex minigame called “hot coffee.” Developers cut the minigame from the final release, but it was still on the physical discs that went to stores. Modders uncovered it in the files and were able to patch it back in.

California politician Leland Yee got wind of the mod and condemned the Entertainment Software Ratings Board (ESRB) for labeling the game “Mature” instead of “Adults Only.” Cable news went wild. Rachel Maddow weighed in. Hillary Clinton, then a Senator in New York, demanded an investigation. Congress voted to send the FTC after Rockstar for deceiving the ESRB. 

The ESRB updated the game’s rating to an AO. Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers . publisher Take-Two shipped new copies with the content completely removed. Take-Two’s shareholders also removed most of its board and put Strauss Zelnick in charge. He’s been the CEO ever since.

— The Ballad of Jack Thompson

The cultural winds had shifted by the time hit stores in 2008. Retailers across the country had midnight release parties where people lined up to purchase the game as soon as possible. Local news outlets interviewed people in line and marveled at how much money might make.

But the culture warriors still pointed to GTA as proof of America’s moral decline. Glenn Beck, then an anchor on CNN Headline News, on the game and often spoke to American lawyer Jack Thompson. Thompson hated Grand Theft Auto so much and was so sure it was training young people to kill their elders that he let his crusade against the franchise ruin his life.

Thompson against Take-Two aimed at preventing the company from selling at all. The publisher counter-sued, Thompson accused it of perjury, and the parties eventually settled. In its ruling, the courts said Thompson could never use the legal system to stop Take-Two from publishing a game ever again.

He didn’t stop though. After the game came out, Thompson Rockstar had based an assassination mission on him. He then sent a letter to Strauss Zelnick’s mom. “Your son, this very moment, is doing everything he possibly can to sell as many copies of GTA IV to teen boys in the United States, a country in which your son claims you raised him to be ‘a Boy Scout.’ More like the Hitler Youth, I would say. Happy Mother’s day, Mrs. Zelnick, which this year is May 11, two weeks after your son unleashes porn and violence upon other mothers’ boys. I'm sure you’re very proud,” Thompson wrote in the letter.

The Supreme Court of Florida permanently disbarred him shortly thereafter.

Money in the Age of Violence

In 2013, made a billion dollars in three days and was the biggest entertainment release of all time. It made more money than any movie, book, album, or video game had ever made before. Every news broadcast about the game led with that fact. “Never has there been an opening like this in the entertainment industry,” CBS News said.

Jake Tapper and CNET’s Dan Ackerman lamented that GTA V’s success would hurt the creativity of the video game industry. “It’s become such a hit-driven business. You have to have a big opening day or opening weekend for anyone to take you seriously. And when you have such a hit-driven business, I think people get risk averse and they don’t get as creative,” Ackerman told Tapper. 

The news still ran segments about the violence and sex in the game, but it was typically couched in a conversation about its runaway financial success. Most anchors brought on experts who told them about the business. They sought to understand what was happening and why people liked the game, rather than condemning it outright. 

Anxieties of American Decline

In 2026, cultural fears about violence and sex in video games are gone. Instead, we’re all worried about money. Everyone is sure will make money, the question is if it will make the money?

“Why the stakes for GTA VI are so high,” declared the thumbnail for a Bloomberg video about the game. The outlet’s podcast also ran an episode about why the . Newsweek worried that the U.S. economy as people take time off work to play. CBS News’ morning show wondered how much money the game would make and the anchor admitted he once “lost a summer” to Grand Theft Auto. No one discussed violence at all. CNBC’s coverage called the game a “Billion Dollar Hype Machine.”

Behind it all is a kind of lament — a worry that might be a final hurrah for this kind of game. Rumors are that it cost a billion dollars. Games are more expensive than ever and the industry has been devastated. A third of the industry lost their jobs in the past 24 months and most of them . Even when a game is successful, companies cut staff. wondered if GTA VI “may be the last great heist.”

Underneath all these economic fears, the older panics still lurked. On Fox News, middling collegiate swimmer turned political activist Riley Gaines hoped that the game’s romantic elements would lead to a rise in birth rates. “Hopefully these men realize they like the feeling of love, romantic love, and go out and find it. Because, I’ll tell you what, we’re in a population decline. We need more babies. You can’t have babies, real babies, mouths to feed, from video games,” Gaines said.

Twitch streamer Sasha Grey had early access to the game and was streaming it to YouTube and Twitch when YouTube shut down her stream for “nudity.” An early cutscene showed what Grey described as “artistic nip and some booty.” Grey complained to YouTube in a post on X and shared a screenshot of the moment the company shut down her stream. 

“They allow far worse under their educational category. This game is art, y’know? It’s the biggest release of the friggin’ decade,” Grey said during her stream. She pulled up the post on X to see if she’d gotten a response. “Oh god, the Twitter post got labeled as adult content, which means it’s going to be harder to get seen.”

The old protestant advertiser-friendly anti-sex morality is still there, programmed into the computer systems we use every day.

items.title: College Board Delivers Another AI Ultimatum: No AI, No AP CS Principles Course
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader theodp writes: Just days after news broke of Google's no AI, no Search ultimatum -- prompting school districts to weigh breaking up with Google Search (source paywalled; alternative source) -- the College Board quietly delivered another AI ultimatum to the nation's AP Computer Science Principles teachers, suggesting that their days of teaching AP CSP might be over unless their school districts put an end to their anti-AI ways.
 
"Effective in fall 2027," The College Board explained, "AP Computer Science Principles has been reimagined as the course for teaching students how to work with AI responsibly, safely, and confidently. AI is integral to the world of computer science. Software engineering remains one of the largest professional job categories, and employers now expect software engineers to be fluent in AI. What sets candidates apart is a deeper understanding of AI for designing, debugging, and evaluating code, and the ability to determine when AI is wrong. The redesigned course develops these skills, empowering students to build with AI, not just learn about it. [...] Students also complete an AI Create Project, in which they build an AI application. The AP Exam includes free-response questions about the project, so students who earn a qualifying score for college credit have demonstrated their ability to design, build, and understand an AI-powered application. [...] Students need access to a district-approved AI tool that accepts a student's own written instructions and returns a response. Schools will need to make sure every student has access to one."
 
The College Board also announced a planned ban on the use of block-based programming languages like Snap!, Scratch, Blockly, and MIT App Inventor for students' "AI Create Project" (which replaces the current "Create Performance Task" that counts for 30% of a student's AP exam score): "Beginning with the 2028-29 school year, students will submit their AI Create Project in one of a limited number of text-based languages. This change aligns the course with introductory college computer science courses, where text-based languages are most commonly used. If you currently teach programming with block-based tools, you can continue to use them in your teaching while introducing text-based languages throughout the year. Students will need to be working in an approved text-based language by the time they submit their AI Create Project in 2028-29."
